b:
I’m currently stewing over $100. Yet I’m remarkably relaxed about a $250 rental car and a $1,300 gearbox rebuild waiting for me after a trip to the Canary Islands of the coast of North Africa. On paper, the math makes no sense, which got me wondering why my brain works this way.
Last week, I did the organized thing and booked long-stay parking at our local airport. Being frugal, I picked the cheapest option: $100 upfront, no refunds, no changes. Days later, my car developed a gearbox issue, and my mechanic told me not to drive it until it’s fixed. So while my wife, Suzie, and I celebrate her 60th birthday in the winter sun, our car will be up on a ramp instead of in the airport lot I paid for.
The $100 is gone. The $250 rental barely registers, because we’re a one-car household by choice. Renting occasionally is far cheaper than taxing, insuring, and maintaining a second vehicle that sits idle in the driveway. Better still, I picked the rental up in my hometown and will drop it at the airport, saving a cab fare. The $1,300 repair is less welcome, but I’ve made peace with it.
So only the smallest of the three bills irritates me. Looking at it through a behavioral lens, I see three reasons why.
First, the $100 bought nothing. The rental gets us around town and to the airport. The rebuild gets me a working car. Both buy something tangible. The parking fee simply evaporated.
Second, I only have myself to blame. I paid early to be prudent, then chose the no-refund rate to save a few dollars, and events promptly overtook that choice. The rental and repair weren’t choices, they just happened to me, and it’s hard to stay mad at bad luck. It’s much harder to forgive a bet you placed yourself.
Third, the $100 has no home. Behavioral finance calls this mental accounting, our habit of sorting money into psychological buckets. The rental goes into “normal operating costs” and the gearbox in “inevitable wear and tear.” The $100 belongs to neither, an irritating little leak in an otherwise tidy plan.
There’s a final twist. I agreed to the terms, so I can’t even claim I was treated unfairly. Paying $1,300 for parts and skilled labor feels like a fair exchange, and $100 for an empty, windswept piece of tarmac is technically fair too. It just doesn’t feel right.
The takeaway? My financial reactions aren’t strictly rational, and after years of managing money, I’m fine with that. The sting of spending rarely comes down to the price tag. It depends on what we get in return and whether we have only ourselves to blame.
There’s no appeal to make, so I’ll raise a glass to Suzie’s 60th and stay mad for a few days, until something else distracts me. Probably trying to convert euros into real money.
